title: Ex(pert) marks the spot
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien reflects on what makes an expert teacher, prompted by Nidhi Sachdeva and Paul Kirschner's conversation on Chalk & Talk about their book Becoming an Expert Teacher. He rejects the idea that teachers are born rather than made and argues that deliberate, targeted practice matters, using Shaquille O'Neal's free-throw work as an example. Teaching is unusual because teachers perform far more than they practise, which makes reflection and incremental improvement hard to find time for. Drawing on his experience in Australia, where teachers often teach outside their degree, he shows how rich domain knowledge supports the instructional decisions experts make when lessons go off plan. He defends pre-made curriculum resources as workload savers that support, but do not replace, expertise. Finally he offers three practical routes to expertise: communities of practice, peer observation with debriefs, and self-authored professional development plans.
points: Expertise comes from specific, targeted practice on known weaknesses, not from generic repetition or innate calling.
Teaching inverts the usual ratio of practice to performance, with perhaps 75 to 80 percent of a teacher's time in service of performing, so improvement must be built in deliberately.
Rich domain-specific knowledge is what lets an expert re-teach a concept several ways and respond when a lesson stops working.
Shared curriculum resources cut workload and free experts to focus on the class in front of them, but they do not remove the need to plan.
Communities of practice, peer observation with a real debrief, and teacher-authored development goals are practical ways to grow expertise.
quotes: The idea that you could be born to be a teacher is severely misguided. Similar to the way we often suggest athletes were born with a disposition and talent which makes them on a level unmatched by any other.

Developing expertise in this space can be challenging because novices through generic practice can make significant gains very quickly into competence, however once an individual is competent is where the importance of specific practice comes into play.

In much of sports training there is what is referred to as the ‘pareto principle’ which states that 80% of your practice should be easy and 20% should be hard. While in teaching we seem to have those numbers reversed

What separates an expert, from a novice, is that all of the past experiences the expert teacher has lived through allows them to use what they’ve learned from and reflected on in all of those challenges and turn that knowledge into the optimal response to the problem at hand.
The key benefit of pre-built curriculum resources is simply that they cut down workload. They do not however, eliminate the need for planning.
Teacher improvement and developing expertise is impossible without a plan. You cannot hope teachers improve solely on good vibes.

The reality of observations is that they are far more beneficial for the observer as they are able to see how strategies look in action and think about how those strategies may look in their own context and the benefit they bring.
